title: Energy systems
examples: Which energy system is best for a long marathon run?
How does the body switch between these energy systems?
What is the main limiting factor for the ATP-PC system?

explain.say: Today we explore how your body makes energy for exercise.

items: High intensity burst: ATP-PC system used
Medium intensity: Glycolytic system kicks in
Low intensity/Long duration: Aerobic system dominates

explain.say: The phosphocreatine system uses stored energy for immediate power.
Glycolysis breaks down glucose without needing oxygen for energy.
Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to fully break down fuel sources.
When you run a mile, you rely mostly on aerobic respiration.
A common mistake is thinking all energy production is instant.

draw.text: Mistake: Thinking energy is always instant

faq.q: What is the main difference between aerobic and anaerobic systems?
faq.a: Aerobic systems require oxygen to produce large amounts of energy over time. Anaerobic systems do not need oxygen and are used for short, intense bursts.
asks: Do I need oxygen for all energy?
What is the role of oxygen in energy?

faq.q: Why do I feel muscle burn during intense exercise?
faq.a: The burning sensation is often related to the buildup of lactic acid from anaerobic glycolysis. This signals that the system is working very hard.
asks: Is lactic acid bad for me?

faq.q: How long can I use the ATP-PC system?
faq.a: The ATP-PC system stores energy very quickly, but it is depleted within about ten seconds of maximal effort. It is for explosive power.
asks: How fast does this energy system run out?

faq.q: Does the body prioritize one system over others?
faq.a: The body adapts by using a combination of systems depending on the intensity and duration of the activity. It shifts as the exercise continues.
asks: Does the body choose the best system?
How does energy system usage change?

faq.q: What is glucose, and where does it come from?
faq.a: Glucose is a simple sugar that is the primary fuel source for energy production. It comes from the carbohydrates we eat.
asks: What fuel do I burn for energy?
Where does the body get sugar?

facts: The ATP-PC system provides energy for the first few seconds of intense activity.
Anaerobic glycolysis produces energy quickly but results in lactic acid.
Aerobic respiration is the most efficient system, using oxygen to maximize ATP yield.
Fuel sources include carbohydrates, fats, and proteins, though carbs are primary for quick energy.

quiz.say: For a 100 meter sprint, which system is dominant?
quiz.why: The sprint is very short and requires maximum immediate power, which the ATP-PC system provides.

wrong.0: Fats are too slow to break down for such an explosive movement.
wrong.2: This system is better for activities lasting longer than a few seconds.
wrong.3: This system requires too much time and oxygen for a short sprint.

quiz.say: Which process produces lactic acid without oxygen?
quiz.why: Glycolysis is the breakdown of glucose that occurs without the presence of oxygen.

wrong.0: Fat oxidation is a slower process that usually occurs aerobically.
wrong.2: Aerobic respiration requires oxygen to complete the energy cycle.
wrong.3: The ATP-PC system uses stored phosphates, not necessarily glycolysis.

quiz.say: When running a marathon, the primary energy source is:
quiz.why: Marathons are long events, requiring the sustained, efficient energy production from aerobic respiration.

wrong.0: Glycolysis builds up waste products too quickly for endurance.
wrong.1: This system cannot sustain energy output for hours.
wrong.3: This system runs out of fuel in under ten seconds.
